{{Short description|Event in dynamical systems theory}}
In [[dynamical systems theory]], a '''period-doubling bifurcation''' occurs when a slight change in a system's parameters causes a new periodic trajectory to emerge from an existing periodic trajectory—the new one having double the period of the original. With the doubled period, it takes twice as long (or, in a [[Discrete time and continuous time|discrete]] dynamical system, twice as many iterations) for the numerical values visited by the system to repeat themselves.

A '''period-halving bifurcation''' occurs when a system switches to a new behavior with half the period of the original system.

A '''period-doubling cascade''' is an infinite sequence of period-doubling bifurcations. Such cascades are one route by which dynamical systems can develop chaos.<ref>Alligood (1996) et al., p. 532</ref> In [[hydrodynamics]], they are one of the possible routes to [[turbulence]].<ref>{{cite book |first1=Kip S.|last1=Thorne|first2=Roger D.|last2=Blandford|author-link1=Kip Thorne|title=Modern Classical Physics: Optics, Fluids, Plasmas, Elasticity, Relativity, and Statistical Physics|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2017|isbn=978-0-691-15902-7|pages=825–834}}</ref>

[[Image:Chaosorderchaos.png|400px|right|thumb|Period-halving bifurcations (L) leading to order, followed by period-doubling bifurcations (R) leading to chaos.]]
==Examples==
[[Image:Logistic Bifurcation map High Resolution.png|thumb|right|300px|[[Bifurcation diagram]] for the logistic map.
It shows the [[attractor|attractor  values]], like <math>x_*</math> and <math>x'_*</math>, as a function of the parameter <math>r</math>.]]

===Logistic map===
The [[logistic map]] is 
:<math>x_{n+1} = r x_n (1 - x_n)</math> 
where <math>x_n</math> is a function of the (discrete) time <math>n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots</math>.<ref>Strogatz (2015), pp. 360–373</ref> The parameter <math>r</math> is assumed to lie in the interval <math>[0,4]</math>, in which case <math>x_n</math> is bounded on <math>[0,1]</math>.

For <math>r</math> between 1 and 3, <math>x_n</math> converges to the stable fixed point <math>x_* = (r-1)/r</math>. Then, for <math>r</math> between 3 and 3.44949, <math>x_n</math> converges to a permanent oscillation between two values <math>x_*</math> and <math>x'_*</math> that depend on <math>r</math>. As <math>r</math> grows larger, oscillations between 4 values, then 8, 16, 32, etc. appear. These period doublings culminate at <math>r \approx 3.56995</math>, beyond which more complex regimes appear. As <math>r</math> increases, there are some intervals where most starting values will converge to one or a small number of stable oscillations, such as near <math>r=3.83</math>, where there is a stable period-three solution.

In the interval where the period is <math>2^n</math> for some positive integer <math>n</math>, not all the points actually have period <math>2^n</math>. These are single points, rather than intervals. These points are said to be in unstable orbits, since nearby points do not approach the same orbit as them.

===Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation===
[[File:K-S equation period doubling.png|thumb|right|600px|Period doubling in the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation with periodic boundary conditions. The curves depict solutions of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation projected onto the energy phase plane ''(E, dE/dt)'', where ''E'' is the [[Lp space|''L<sup>2</sup>''-norm]] of the solution. For ''ν'' = 0.056, there exists a periodic orbit with period ''T'' ≈ 1.1759. Near ''ν'' ≈ 0.0558, this solution splits into 2 orbits, which further separate as ''ν'' is decreased. Exactly at the transitional value of ''ν'', the new orbit (red-dashed) has double the period of the original. (However, as ''ν'' increases further, the ratio of periods deviates from exactly 2.)]]
The [[Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation]] is an example of a spatiotemporally continuous dynamical system that exhibits period doubling. It is one of the most well-studied nonlinear [[partial differential equation]]s, originally introduced as a model of flame front propagation.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kalogirou|first1=A.|last2=Keaveny|first2=E. E.|last3=Papageorgiou|first3=D. T.|title=An in-depth numerical study of the two-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=471|issue=2179|year=2015|article-number=20140932|issn=1364-5021|doi=10.1098/rspa.2014.0932|pmid=26345218|pmc=4528647|bibcode=2015RSPSA.47140932K }}</ref>

The one-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation is
:<math>
u_t + u u_x + u_{xx} + \nu \, u_{xxxx} = 0
</math>
A common choice for boundary conditions is spatial periodicity: <math>u(x + 2 \pi, t) = u(x,t)</math>.

For large values of <math>\nu</math>, <math>u(x,t)</math> evolves toward steady (time-independent) solutions or simple periodic orbits. As <math>\nu</math> is decreased, the dynamics eventually develops chaos. The transition from order to chaos occurs via a cascade of period-doubling bifurcations,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Smyrlis|first1=Y. S.|last2=Papageorgiou|first2=D. T.|title=Predicting chaos for infinite dimensional dynamical systems: the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a case study.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=88|issue=24|year=1991|pages=11129–11132|issn=0027-8424|doi=10.1073/pnas.88.24.11129|pmid=11607246|pmc=53087|bibcode=1991PNAS...8811129S |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last1 = Papageorgiou|first1 = D.T.|last2 = Smyrlis|first2 = Y.S.|year = 1991|title = The route to chaos for the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation|journal =  Theoretical and Computational Fluid Dynamics|volume = 3| issue=1 |pages = 15–42|doi = 10.1007/BF00271514| bibcode=1991ThCFD...3...15P | hdl=2060/19910004329 | s2cid=116955014 |issn = 1432-2250|hdl-access = free}}</ref> one of which is illustrated in the figure.

===Logistic map for a modified Phillips curve===

Consider the following logistical map for a modified [[Phillips curve]]: 

<math> \pi_{t} = f(u_{t}) + b \pi_{t}^e </math>

<math> \pi_{t+1} = \pi_{t}^e + c (\pi_{t} - \pi_{t}^e) </math>

<math> f(u) = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} e^{-u} \,</math>

<math> b > 0, 0 \leq c \leq 1, \frac {df} {du} < 0 </math>

where :
* <math>\pi</math> is the actual [[inflation]]
*  <math> \pi^e </math> is the expected inflation, 
* u is the level of unemployment, 
* <math> m - \pi </math> is the [[money supply]] growth rate. 

Keeping <math> \beta_{1} = -2.5, \ \beta_{2} = 20, \ c = 0.75 </math> and varying <math>b</math>, the system undergoes period-doubling bifurcations and ultimately becomes chaotic.{{cn|date=February 2021}}

==Experimental observation==
Period doubling has been observed in a number of experimental systems.<ref> see Strogatz (2015) for a review</ref> There is also experimental evidence of period-doubling cascades. For example, sequences of 4 period doublings have been observed in the dynamics of [[convection rolls]] in water and [[Mercury (element)|mercury]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Giglio|first1=Marzio|last2=Musazzi|first2=Sergio|last3=Perini|first3=Umberto|title=Transition to Chaotic Behavior via a Reproducible Sequence of Period-Doubling Bifurcations|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=47|issue=4|year=1981|pages=243–246|issn=0031-9007|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.47.243|bibcode=1981PhRvL..47..243G }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Libchaber|first1=A.|last2=Laroche|first2=C.|last3=Fauve|first3=S.|title=Period doubling cascade in mercury, a quantitative measurement|journal=Journal de Physique Lettres|volume=43|issue=7|year=1982|pages=211–216|issn=0302-072X|doi=10.1051/jphyslet:01982004307021100|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/jpa-00232033/file/ajp-jphyslet_1982_43_7_211_0.pdf}}</ref> Similarly, 4-5 doublings have been observed in certain nonlinear [[electronic circuit]]s.<ref name="Linsay1981">{{cite journal|last1=Linsay|first1=Paul S.|title=Period Doubling and Chaotic Behavior in a Driven Anharmonic Oscillator|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=47|issue=19|year=1981|pages=1349–1352|issn=0031-9007|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.47.1349|bibcode=1981PhRvL..47.1349L }}</ref><ref name="TestaPérez1982">{{cite journal|last1=Testa|first1=James|last2=Pérez|first2=José|last3=Jeffries|first3=Carson|title=Evidence for Universal Chaotic Behavior of a Driven Nonlinear Oscillator|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=48|issue=11|year=1982|pages=714–717|issn=0031-9007|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.48.714|bibcode=1982PhRvL..48..714T |url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/18m504mf}}</ref><ref name="ArecchiLisi1982">{{cite journal|last1=Arecchi|first1=F. T.|last2=Lisi|first2=F.|title=Hopping Mechanism Generating1fNoise in Nonlinear Systems|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=49|issue=2|year=1982|pages=94–98|issn=0031-9007|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.94|bibcode=1982PhRvL..49...94A }}</ref> However, the experimental precision required to detect the ''i''<sup>th</sup> doubling event in a cascade increases exponentially with ''i'', making it difficult to observe more than 5 doubling events in a cascade.<ref>Strogatz (2015), pp. 360–373</ref>
